entry.title: What Pre-LLM NLP Got Right About Meaning

link.title: What Pre-LLM NLP Got Right About Meaning

entry.content:
— and what we lost when we stopped looking at tasks

Bigger language models don’t automatically lead to better understanding, and the rise of LLMs makes tasks, specialized corpora, and human evaluation more important than ever.

Large language models changed how we interact with language.

They generate fluent text, metaphors, poems, explanations — often with a level of surface competence that would have seemed impossible only a few years ago. As a result, our collective understanding of what it means for a system to “understand language” has shifted dramatically.

And yet, something subtle has been lost along the way.

Before LLMs, NLP was not more powerful. But in some important ways, it was clearer about what it was trying to understand. Meaning was not assumed to be an emergent property of scale. It was something that had to be defined, constrained, and tested — often imperfectly, but explicitly.

When NLP was built around tasks

Pre-LLM NLP was structured around tasks. These tasks were sometimes narrow, sometimes artificial, often frustrating — but they forced clarity.

A task required researchers to specify what counted as success, under which conditions, and for which kind of language use. Parsing, similarity judgments, metaphor identification, sentiment evaluation, reading times, and human ratings were not just benchmarks. They were ways of making meaning observable.

Meaning was never taken for granted. It had to be operationalized.

This led to workflows that now look heavy or slow: carefully designed stimuli, controlled datasets, handcrafted features, and human evaluation at every step. But this constraint had an important consequence. Models were never detached from the phenomena they were meant to capture. They were tied — sometimes uncomfortably — to specific questions about human language behavior.

Measuring meaning through human behavior

My own work emerged from that tradition.

In one peer-reviewed study, we used eye-tracking to investigate how people read a real French poem — Baudelaire’s Les Chats. The linguistic content of the poem never changed. Only its visual presentation did: verse versus prose.

The effect was immediate and measurable. Readers spent more time, reread more often, and processed rhyme differently when the poem appeared in its original verse form.

Nothing about the semantics had changed. What changed was how meaning was experienced.

This kind of result is difficult to detect if we only evaluate output quality or textual plausibility. But it becomes visible when meaning is approached through human behavior: eye movements, hesitation, rereading, attention allocation. Meaning, in this view, is not only semantic content. It emerges from form, sound, layout, expectation, and task.

From eye movements to metaphor and beauty

Later, during my PhD work, I extended this logic to a larger scale.

Instead of a single poem, I worked with an ecological corpus of French literature, from which I constructed a specialized poetry subcorpus. Using NLP tools, I extracted candidate metaphorical phrases based on syntactic patterns, validated them with expert judgments, and tested them in large-scale online studies involving 1,500 participants.

Participants rated short phrases on comprehension, familiarity, beauty, and metaphoricity.

Once again, the goal was not to label metaphors automatically. It was to ask a more fundamental question: which measurable properties of language shape human judgments?

The results were strikingly consistent. Beauty and metaphoricity clustered together, while comprehension and familiarity formed a separate cluster. Judgments were shaped by semantic similarity, sound structure, aesthetic potential, and syntactic form. Familiarity mattered — but not linearly. Extreme familiarity and extreme unfamiliarity led to confident judgments, while intermediate familiarity produced ambiguity and hesitation.

What emerged was a graded picture of meaning. Metaphoricity and beauty were not subjective noise. They were structured responses to identifiable properties of language.

What pre-LLM NLP understood well

Looking back, several principles stand out.

First, meaning was never reduced to a single score. It was decomposed into multiple dimensions — similarity, affect, familiarity, imagery, effort, aesthetics — even when the models themselves were simple.

Second, human evaluation was not optional. Eye movements, reaction times, and ratings were not treated as secondary validation. They were taken as reference, because they reflect actual human behavioral responses to linguistic stimuli. Meaning was inferred from how people read, hesitate, reread, and judge — not from model output alone.

Third, tasks anchored interpretation. A task forced researchers to define success with explicit control and constraints. It made clear what was being tested, under which conditions, and for whom. Without a task, “understanding” quickly became rhetorical rather than empirical.

Finally, interpretability mattered. Features were not only tools for prediction. They were designed to be understood, criticized, and revised. Modeling was as much about insight as it was about performance.

What changed in the post-LLM shift

LLMs are extraordinary, but their success altered our habits.

In many applied settings — demos, prototypes, and parts of the research discourse — explicit tasks are increasingly replaced by prompts, and evaluation drifts toward qualitative impressions. Fluency becomes a proxy for meaning. Aesthetic quality is treated as an emergent property rather than something that can be analyzed.

We gained flexibility and scale. But we lost explicit operational constraints.

Without those constraints, it becomes harder to explain why a system works, harder to distinguish comprehension from engagement, harder to separate beauty from coherence, and harder to notice when models perform well for the wrong reasons.

LLMs can produce metaphors beautifully. But producing language is not the same as modeling the conditions under which humans find something metaphorical or beautiful.

Bigger isn’t always better — it’s often blurrier

Scale has undeniable advantages. But it also has costs.

When everything is included in the training data, genre distinctions soften and signals that matter for specific kinds of language use are averaged out. This is especially problematic for poetry and metaphor, where meaning depends on rare but meaningful patterns.

Metaphor relies on a delicate balance. Expressions must be unfamiliar enough to create surprise, yet familiar enough to be interpretable as metaphorical rather than nonsensical. When language is treated as a homogeneous mass, this balance is blurred. Rare constructions lose their distinctiveness, and the very patterns that carry aesthetic and figurative force are diluted.

For tasks involving interpretation, aesthetic judgment, or expert reading, bigger datasets are not necessarily better datasets. What matters is not coverage, but relevance — relevance to a genre, a reader, a context, and a task.

Pre-LLM NLP made this trade-off explicit. It optimized for alignment rather than sheer volume.

When smaller, specialized corpora made more sense

This difference is especially visible in how data was treated.

Instead of collecting as much text as possible, pre-LLM approaches often relied on highly specific corpora, explicitly aligned with a particular task and a particular human experience. In my own work, this meant starting from a broad literary corpus and then constructing a poetry-focused subcorpus designed to approximate what a reader actually encounters when reading poetry.

The aim was not to model “language in general.” It was to model language as experienced by a reader, in a specific situation, with particular expectations and interpretive habits.

That choice shaped everything downstream. It determined which features were meaningful, which judgments were interpretable, and which questions could even be asked. Familiarity, rarity, sound, and syntactic form mattered precisely because they were evaluated within a constrained and coherent linguistic space.

Meaning was not extracted after the fact. It was encoded into the data design itself.

Why this logic is quietly returning

Interestingly, this task-aligned approach is re-emerging under new names.

Retrieval-augmented generation reintroduces task-specific corpora. Small and local language models favor specialization over generality. On-device systems reduce data circulation and energy costs while prioritizing relevance.

Rather than choosing between handcrafted pipelines and large models, we can now combine curated corpora, explicit task definitions, smaller or local models, and transparent evaluation. This opens the door to systems that are not only fluent, but aligned with specific users and experiences.

Sustainability is part of the equation

There is also an environmental and ethical dimension to this shift.

Running massive models for every query consumes significant energy, centralizes infrastructure, and externalizes environmental cost. Task-specific systems, by contrast, can often run locally, rely on smaller models, and use curated knowledge that is directly relevant to the question being asked.

From this perspective, specialization is not only cognitively sound. It is more sustainable.

Designing systems that know less, but know it better, can be a responsible technical choice.

Meaning lives at the task level

The lesson from pre-LLM NLP is not that large models are wrong.

It is that meaning does not exist independently of tasks.

If we care about understanding, trust, aesthetics, and human experience, we need to keep designing systems where the corpus fits the task, the model fits the context, and evaluation reflects human behavior.

A bridge, not a rejection

This is not an argument against LLMs. It is an argument for continuity.

The future of NLP is not pre-LLM or post-LLM. It is large models combined with well-defined tasks, interpretable features, human evaluation, and respect for how meaning actually shows up in people.

The old questions still matter.
We simply have better tools now — if we choose to use them carefully.

This article draws on peer-reviewed eye-tracking research, large-scale human evaluation studies, and pre-LLM NLP methodologies. I write about language, AI, data, and human judgment — from both technical and lived perspectives.

entry.title: Why Metaphoricity and Beauty Are Entangled

link.title: Why Metaphoricity and Beauty Are Entangled

entry.content:
How sound, familiarity, and semantics shape metaphor judgments

This work comes from a pre-LLM NLP approach combining corpus construction, feature engineering, and large-scale human evaluation.

Evidence from 952 Participants

When people call a phrase “metaphorical,” they often also call it “beautiful.”

This intuition shows up everywhere — in poetry, advertising, and everyday language — but it raises a deeper question:

Are metaphoricity and beauty actually the same judgment, or do they just travel together?

During my PhD, I explored this question using ecologically sourced metaphors, computational linguistic features, and large-scale human ratings. In this article, I’ll focus on what the data revealed when metaphors were presented in isolation, without context.
It is built on earlier peer-reviewed research where I used eye-tracking to study how formal features of French poetry (such as visual layout and rhyme) shape real-time reading behavior, even when textual content remains unchanged.

The experiment in a nutshell

We ran a large online study during the COVID period with 952 French-speaking participants.

Participants rated short phrases extracted from French poetry, selected automatically using syntactic patterns (described in [Article 1]). Each phrase was evaluated on four dimensions:

  • Comprehension
  • Familiarity
  • Beauty
  • Metaphoricity

The material consisted of:

  • 60 metaphorical phrases
  • 60 non-metaphorical phrases

All phrases shared the same syntactic structures (e.g. N de N, N être N, Adj N), allowing us to control form while letting meaning vary naturally.

Two clusters, not four independent judgments

The first striking result was not about metaphors per se — it was about how people use rating scales.

Across participants, the ratings formed two robust clusters:

  • Comprehension ↔ Familiarity
  • Beauty ↔ Metaphoricity

In other words:

  • phrases that were easy to understand were also familiar
  • phrases judged highly metaphorical were often judged beautiful

This pattern appeared consistently, even before any modeling.

This already suggests that metaphoricity is not evaluated purely as a semantic property, but as something that carries aesthetic weight.

Modeling metaphoricity: what actually matters?

To go beyond correlations, we modeled metaphoricity judgments using a combination of:

  • affective–semantic features (e.g. aesthetic potential)
  • sound-based features (e.g. sonority)
  • corpus-derived semantic similarity
  • syntactic pattern type
  • familiarity (modeled non-linearly)

The same predictors emerged repeatedly — whether we modeled: metaphors alone, non-metaphors alone, or the full dataset together.

The strongest contributors were:

  • Aesthetic potential
  • Semantic similarity (distributional, corpus-based)
  • Sonority
  • Syntactic construction
  • A composite affective–aesthetic index adapted from Arthur Jacobs’ neurocognitive poetics framework

Crucially, familiarity mattered only at the extremes: very familiar or very unfamiliar phrases were judged confidently, while mid-range familiarity led to more ambiguity.

A key insight: metaphors and non-metaphors use the same dimensions

One might expect metaphors and non-metaphors to rely on entirely different cues.

They didn’t.

Participants appeared to use the same dimensions — sound, aesthetics, semantic distance, familiarity — for both kinds of phrases. What differed was how strongly those dimensions were weighted.

This supports a graded view of metaphoricity: metaphoricity is not a binary switch it emerges from a combination of interacting properties aesthetic features are part of the signal, not a by-product

Why familiarity behaves strangely (and why that’s interesting)

Familiarity did not show a simple linear effect.

Instead:

  • highly familiar phrases were quickly categorized (often as non-metaphorical)
  • highly unfamiliar phrases were also quickly categorized (often as metaphorical)
  • phrases in between generated hesitation

This pattern aligns with:

  • Relevance Theory (broader interpretation space under uncertainty)
  • foregrounding accounts in literary processing

In other words, effort and ambiguity arise not from novelty alone, but from intermediate predictability.

What this says about beauty

Beauty was not “just noise.”

Many of the same predictors that explained metaphoricity also explained beauty judgments:

  • aesthetic potential
  • sonority
  • semantic relations

This doesn’t mean beauty is metaphoricity — but it suggests that metaphors recruit aesthetic processing early, even when presented without context.

Metaphoricity, in this sense, is not only about meaning transfer. It’s also about how language sounds, feels, and invites interpretation.

Why this matters beyond metaphor studies

These results have broader implications:

  • For psycholinguistics, they support models where figurative meaning emerges from multiple interacting cues.
  • For computational NLP, they highlight the value of interpretable features over single-score metaphor detectors.
  • For aesthetic language research, they show that beauty judgments are not epiphenomenal — they are part of meaning construction.

In a field increasingly dominated by end-to-end models, this kind of work reminds us that understanding language still requires carefully designed tasks and human judgments.

What comes next

In a second study, we examined these same metaphors in context, to test how surrounding text reshapes metaphoricity and beauty judgments.

Context changes many things — but not everything.

That story is for another article.

This work comes from a pre-LLM NLP approach combining corpus construction, feature engineering, and large-scale human evaluation. If you’re interested in experimental NLP, language aesthetics, or metaphor processing, I’ll be sharing more insights from this project.

entry.title: How I Extracted Metaphors from French Poetry (Without Handpicking Them)

link.title: How I Extracted Metaphors from French Poetry (Without Handpicking Them)

entry.content:
A pre-LLM NLP approach using syntactic patterns, poetry corpora, and expert annotation

Most experimental studies on metaphor rely on a familiar trick: researchers construct sentences that are either metaphorical or literal, carefully matching them word by word.

This approach is convenient. It’s also deeply artificial.

During my PhD, I wanted to study metaphor processing using ecological language — metaphors as they actually appear in texts people read for meaning and beauty, not metaphors engineered in a lab. That led me to a deceptively simple question:

How can we select metaphors automatically, at scale, while keeping control over linguistic form?

This article explains the method I developed to do exactly that, using French poetry, syntactic patterns, and expert validation — without handpicking examples or writing “literal controls” by hand.

This work builds on earlier peer-reviewed research where I used eye-tracking to study how formal features of French poetry (such as visual layout and rhyme) shape real-time reading behavior, even when textual content remains unchanged.

Why ecological metaphors are hard to study

Metaphor research has a long tradition of norming metaphorical expressions on dimensions like familiarity, imageability, comprehensibility, or metaphoricity (e.g. Katz et al., 1988; Cardillo et al., 2010; Jacobs & Kinder, 2017).

The problem is that most datasets rely on:

constructed metaphors paired with constructed literal paraphrases

This introduces several issues:

  • Literal “controls” often sound unnatural
  • Register and style subtly change between conditions
  • Syntactic structure is rarely identical
  • The researcher’s intuition heavily shapes the material

In other words, we gain experimental control but lose ecological validity.

Poetry, on the other hand, is full of metaphors — but it’s messy. You can’t just scrape a poetry corpus and label everything metaphorical. You need a way to constrain the search without imposing meaning by hand.

The core idea: control syntax, not meaning

Instead of trying to define metaphors semantically, I flipped the problem.

I asked:

Can we select candidate metaphors automatically by constraining their syntactic form, and let meaning emerge from human judgments?

The intuition was simple:

  • Certain syntactic constructions are highly productive in metaphorical language
  • Those same constructions also appear in non-metaphorical uses
  • If we control syntax, we can compare metaphorical vs non-metaphorical expressions without rewriting them

Step 1: Start with an ecological corpus

I worked with a corpus of French poetry, chosen deliberately:

  • rich in figurative language
  • stylistically diverse
  • far from everyday “lab language”

The goal was not to model poetry per se, but to use it as a high-density source of metaphors.

The corpus was:

  • POS-tagged
  • syntactically parsed

This allowed systematic pattern extraction rather than manual reading.

Step 2: Extract candidate phrases using syntactic patterns

I focused on three simple but powerful constructions:

  • Noun de Noun
    la prison du silence (“the prison of silence”)
  • Noun “être” Noun
    le temps est un fleuve (“time is a river”)
  • Adjective Noun
    une lumière cruelle (“a cruel light”)

These patterns are:

  • frequent in poetry
  • compact (short phrases)
  • compatible with both literal and metaphorical interpretations

Using parsing + POS tagging, I automatically extracted thousands of candidate phrases matching these templates.

At this stage, nothing was labeled metaphorical yet.

Step 3: Random sampling to avoid cherry-picking

From the extracted candidates, I randomly sampled 1,000 phrases.

This step was crucial:

  • no aesthetic preselection
  • no “nice metaphors only”
  • no intuition-driven filtering

Random sampling ensured that the dataset reflected the actual distribution of language in the corpus — including awkward, banal, or ambiguous phrases.

Step 4: Expert validation (meaning, not form)

To determine which phrases were metaphorical, I relied on expert judgments.

  • 4 independent experts evaluated each phrase
  • Each item was labeled as metaphorical or non-metaphorical
  • Only items with high agreement (3/4 or 4/4) were retained

This resulted in:

  • 60 metaphors
  • 60 non-metaphors

All sharing the same syntactic patterns, all drawn from the same poetic sources.

At no point did we rewrite, paraphrase, or “correct” the phrases.

Why this matters methodologically

This approach has several advantages:

1. Ecological validity

All items come from real texts, written for expressive purposes — not experimental convenience.

2. Controlled form

By holding syntax constant, we reduce confounds related to sentence structure, length, or grammatical complexity.

3. Meaning emerges from data

Metaphoricity is not imposed by the researcher, but emerges from expert and participant judgments.

4. Scalability

The method is semi-automatic and reproducible. With different corpora, it can be adapted to:

  • other genres
  • other languages
  • other figurative constructions

What comes next (beyond extraction)

These extracted metaphors were later used in large-scale online studies (around 1,500 participants) where people rated each phrase on:

  • comprehension
  • familiarity
  • beauty
  • metaphoricity

Because the material was ecologically grounded, the results revealed patterns that are often blurred in constructed stimuli — particularly the close relationship between aesthetic judgment and metaphoricity.

That part deserves its own article.

Why I still care about this approach today

In the age of large language models, it’s tempting to think that manual corpus work is obsolete.

I think the opposite is true.

LLMs are powerful because they absorb massive amounts of human language — but they don’t tell us why certain expressions feel metaphorical, beautiful, or striking. For that, we still need:

  • carefully designed stimuli
  • interpretable features
  • human judgments
  • and methods that respect how language is actually used

This metaphor extraction pipeline was my attempt to do exactly that.

If you’re interested in experimental NLP, psycholinguistics, or the intersection of language, meaning, and aesthetics, I’ll be sharing more work from this project — including large-scale behavioral results and modeling insights.

entry.title: a post with plotly.js
entry.content:
This is an example post with some plotly code.

```plotly
{
  "data": [
    {
      "x": [1, 2, 3, 4],
      "y": [10, 15, 13, 17],
      "type": "scatter"
    },
    {
      "x": [1, 2, 3, 4],
      "y": [16, 5, 11, 9],
      "type": "scatter"
    }
  ]
}
```

Which generates:

{
  "data": [
    {
      "x": [1, 2, 3, 4],
      "y": [10, 15, 13, 17],
      "type": "scatter"
    },
    {
      "x": [1, 2, 3, 4],
      "y": [16, 5, 11, 9],
      "type": "scatter"
    }
  ]
}

Also another example chart.

```plotly
{
  "data": [
    {
      "x": [1, 2, 3, 4],
      "y": [10, 15, 13, 17],
      "mode": "markers"
    },
    {
      "x": [2, 3, 4, 5],
      "y": [16, 5, 11, 9],
      "mode": "lines"
    },
    {
      "x": [1, 2, 3, 4],
      "y": [12, 9, 15, 12],
      "mode": "lines+markers"
    }
  ],
  "layout": {
    "title": {
      "text": "Line and Scatter Plot"
    }
  }
}
```

This is how it looks like:

{
  "data": [
    {
      "x": [1, 2, 3, 4],
      "y": [10, 15, 13, 17],
      "mode": "markers"
    },
    {
      "x": [2, 3, 4, 5],
      "y": [16, 5, 11, 9],
      "mode": "lines"
    },
    {
      "x": [1, 2, 3, 4],
      "y": [12, 9, 15, 12],
      "mode": "lines+markers"
    }
  ],
  "layout": {
    "title": {
      "text": "Line and Scatter Plot"
    }
  }
}

entry.title: Are we already in the Brave New World of AI? — Personal Reflections and Ethical Considerations

link.title: Are we already in the Brave New World of AI? — Personal Reflections and Ethical Considerations

entry.content:
Are we already in the Brave New World of AI? — Personal Reflections and Ethical Considerations

✨ Why Read This? ✨

  • Gain personal insights into balancing professional aspirations with ethical considerations.
  • Understand the implications of our society’s shift from mass production to hyper-personalization and how AI amplifies that.
  • Reflect on your role in shaping ethical AI practices and creating a sustainable future.

Let’s ignite meaningful conversations and inspire positive change in the AI landscape.

Today, I had a chain of little moments that made me reflect deeply on my professional journey and its impact on my daughter. The day began with a reflective walk in the 27°C heat at 8 am, dropping my daughter off at kindergarten. This walk, filled with eco-anxiety — thanks to Montreal’s current heat wave, made me realize the importance of finding sustainable and fulfilling work to inspire her, demonstrating strength and confidence by example. I asked myself how I wanted to contribute to the future society she will be a part of.

Back home, a routine conversation with a bank representative unexpectedly turned into a profound discussion about finding meaningful employment. Her straightforward advice struck a chord with me. Later, during my daily content review, I watched a webinar on using AI to automate time-consuming tasks. While insightful, it was clearly a sales pitch, and I was dismayed to discover a tracker installed in my Google account afterward. Not cool.

In parallel, I was developing an AI tool to organize files — an exciting project that helps streamline digital clutter. Thus, it is totally locally on your machine (a critical point if you read this article to the end!). Meanwhile, I listened to a podcast by Asma Mhalla (Yes, you could use an AI tool if you feel that the podcast is too long and you want a summary or because it is in French, I let you check the many possible apps, tools, and their friends developed for that already), which profoundly impacted me. Mhalla discussed our society’s shift from mass production to hyper-personalization, where we are individually targeted yet treated with the same algorithms.

Even more unsettling is how well Google knows us. We have no filter with it, no need to impress or lie. We are constantly bombarded with ads, monitored, and mapped out like discovered territories. Numerous apps now use AI to assist us with everything — from voicing WhatsApp messages to responding to emails and correcting our grammar. While these tools save time and are beneficial when used well, we give these apps everything. Isn’t that concerning?

This brings me to a crucial point: AI tools can significantly enhance our lives by saving time and increasing efficiency, but this convenience comes at the cost of our data privacy.

Free AI is not viable. Large language models require massive storage, and each query consumes significant energy and space. Companies aren’t offering these services for free out of goodwill; they are lucrative enterprises seeking profit. They will eventually monetize through data sales or subscription fees. As data scientists and AI enthusiasts, we must be vigilant about whom we trust with our information.

AI holds incredible potential for positive impact, but it also poses ethical challenges that we cannot ignore. We need to consider our role in this rapidly evolving landscape carefully. As professionals, it’s our responsibility to navigate these complexities and advocate for ethical AI practices.

Let’s take a moment to reflect on our journey in this exciting yet daunting field. How can we contribute to a future where AI serves humanity ethically and responsibly with sustainability? Your thoughts and insights are invaluable in shaping this dialogue.

Feel free to share your experiences and join the conversation. Together, we can pave the way for a more ethical and inspiring AI-driven future!

entry.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

link.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

entry.content:
Learn more:Learn more:Learn more:Learn more:Learn more:Learn more:May 14, 2024 We’re introducing a series of updates across the Gemini family of models, including the new 1.5 Flash, our lightweight model for speed and efficiency, and Project Astra, our vision for the future of AI assistants. In December, we launched our first natively multimodal model Gemini 1.0 in three sizes: Ultra, Pro and Nano. Just a few months later we released 1.5 Pro, with enhanced performance and a breakthrough long context window of 1 million tokens.Developers and enterprise customers have been putting 1.5 Pro to use in incredible ways and finding its long context window, multimodal reasoning capabilities and impressive overall performance incredibly useful.We know from user feedback that some applications need lower latency and a lower cost to serve. This inspired us to keep innovating, so today, we’re introducing Gemini 1.5 Flash: a model that’s lighter-weight than 1.5 Pro, and designed to be fast and efficient to serve at scale.Both 1.5 Pro and 1.5 Flash are available in public preview with a 1 million token context window in Google AI Studio and Vertex AI. And now, 1.5 Pro is also available with a 2 million token context window via waitlist to developers using the API and to Google Cloud customers.We’re also introducing updates across the Gemini family of models, announcing our next generation of open models, Gemma 2, and sharing progress on the future of AI assistants, with Project Astra.Context lengths of leading foundation models compared with Gemini 1.5’s 2 million token capability1.5 Flash is the newest addition to the Gemini model family and the fastest Gemini model served in the API. It’s optimized for high-volume, high-frequency tasks at scale, is more cost-efficient to serve and features our breakthrough long context window.While it’s a lighter weight model than 1.5 Pro, it’s highly capable of multimodal reasoning across vast amounts of information and delivers impressive quality for its size.The new Gemini 1.5 Flash model is optimized for speed and efficiency, is highly capable of multimodal reasoning and features our breakthrough long context window.1.5 Flash excels at summarization, chat applications, image and video captioning, data extraction from long documents and tables, and more. This is because it’s been trained by 1.5 Pro through a process called “distillation,” where the most essential knowledge and skills from a larger model are transferred to a smaller, more efficient model.Read more about 1.5 Flash in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report, on the Gemini technology page, and learn about 1.5 Flash’s availability and pricing.Over the last few months, we’ve significantly improved 1.5 Pro, our best model for general performance across a wide range of tasks.Beyond extending its context window to 2 million tokens, we’ve enhanced its code generation, logical reasoning and planning, multi-turn conversation, and audio and image understanding through data and algorithmic advances. We see strong improvements on public and internal benchmarks for each of these tasks.1.5 Pro can now follow increasingly complex and nuanced instructions, including ones that specify product-level behavior involving role, format and style. We’ve improved control over the model’s responses for specific use cases, like crafting the persona and response style of a chat agent or automating workflows through multiple function calls. And we’ve enabled users to steer model behavior by setting system instructions.We added audio understanding in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, so 1.5 Pro can now reason across image and audio for videos uploaded in Google AI Studio. And we’re now integrating 1.5 Pro into Google products, including Gemini Advanced and in Workspace apps.Read more about 1.5 Pro in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report and on the Gemini technology page.Gemini Nano is expanding beyond text-only inputs to include images as well. Starting with Pixel, applications using Gemini Nano with Multimodality will be able to understand the world the way people do — not just through text, but also through sight, sound and spoken language.Read more about Gemini 1.0 Nano on Android.Today, we’re also sharing a series of updates to Gemma, our family of open models built from the same research and technology used to create the Gemini models.We’re announcing Gemma 2, our next generation of open models for responsible AI innovation. Gemma 2 has a new architecture designed for breakthrough performance and efficiency, and will be available in new sizes.The Gemma family is also expanding with PaliGemma, our first vision-language model inspired by PaLI-3. And we’ve upgraded our Responsible Generative AI Toolkit with LLM Comparator for evaluating the quality of model responses.Read more on the Developer blog.As part of Google DeepMind’s mission to build AI responsibly to benefit humanity, we’ve always wanted to develop universal AI agents that can be helpful in everyday life. That’s why today, we’re sharing our progress in building the future of AI assistants with Project Astra (advanced seeing and talking responsive agent).To be truly useful, an agent needs to understand and respond to the complex and dynamic world just like people do — and take in and remember what it sees and hears to understand context and take action. It also needs to be proactive, teachable and personal, so users can talk to it naturally and without lag or delay.While we’ve made incredible progress developing AI systems that can understand multimodal information, getting response time down to something conversational is a difficult engineering challenge. Over the past few years, we’ve been working to improve how our models perceive, reason and converse to make the pace and quality of interaction feel more natural.Building on Gemini, we’ve developed prototype agents that can process information faster by continuously encoding video frames, combining the video and speech input into a timeline of events, and caching this information for efficient recall.By leveraging our leading speech models, we also enhanced how they sound, giving the agents a wider range of intonations. These agents can better understand the context they’re being used in, and respond quickly, in conversation.With technology like this, it’s easy to envision a future where people could have an expert AI assistant by their side, through a phone or glasses. And some of these capabilities are coming to Google products, like the Gemini app and web experience, later this year.We’ve made incredible progress so far with our family of Gemini models, and we’re always striving to advance the state-of-the-art even further. By investing in a relentless production line of innovation, we’re able to explore new ideas at the frontier, while also unlocking the possibility of new and exciting Gemini use cases.Learn more about Gemini and its capabilities. entry.title: DIY AI: Crafting Your Llamapal Personal Agent Has Never Been Easier!

link.title: DIY AI: Crafting Your Llamapal Personal Agent Has Never Been Easier!

entry.content:
Throughout my life, from school presentations to my PhD pursuits, curating comprehensive summaries has been a significant time commitment. The initial rush of gathering diverse sources feels like a surge of excitement, akin to a sugar rush of newfound knowledge. Using Evernote, I meticulously organize my findings, creating a structured database for crafting summaries and gaining insights (Yes, color-classified and annotated). However, the sheer research volume can overwhelm once the initial excitement fades. A sophisticated LLM interface would have been invaluable, offering information retrieval, analysis, categorization, and summarization capabilities. Imagine a tool capable of quickly digesting hundreds of documents! With assistants like LlamaPal (or LP, for friends), the prospect of revolutionizing information management is exhilarating, enhancing the writing process with genuine utility.

Personalization is critical to provide tailored user experiences in AI assistants. One powerful approach to achieve this is to enrich pre-trained large language models (LLMs) with personal data. In this blog post, we’ll explore the process of creating a personalized AI assistant using Langchain, highlighting the crucial role of quantization and alternative libraries in developing a Retriever-Reader model (RAG).

This is a two-part project. This article presents the theoretical workflow to construct an assistant in a proof-of-concept code. Leveraging the latest advancements, I present the different steps to consider in building a personal agent and the possible options. In the second article, I will present the code in more detail. This project accommodates various information inputs tailored to your needs, presenting vast potential for applications in professional endeavors, skill acquisition, persuasive discourse, or simply for recreational purposes.

First, you must choose a LLM to build a personal agent on your computer. Which one? That is a fundamental question, and it depends on many criteria. Of course, the state of the art is considered the GPT-4 model. However, it is pretty costly (see Figure). We use llama here for the code examples. Of course, you can also check those resources for more information on the available LLM (see Saplig and HELM). We could also use open-source models like Falcon, Bloom, or gpt-Neox—others like Mistral, RoBERTa, Claude, etc. There are many possibilities depending on your task, the power of your machine and space, your finances, and the implementation you can use, as all the models are not available with all the options I present in this article. Some choices could reduce your possibilities.

  1. Quantization: Optimizing Model Loading Efficiency

Quantization plays a pivotal role in optimizing the efficiency of our AI assistant. By reducing the numerical precision of the model’s weights, we can significantly decrease memory and computational requirements, making the model more efficient, especially on hardware with limited resources. However, it’s crucial to acknowledge that this optimization may also impact the model’s accuracy. There are several approaches to quantization.

Different options lie ahead of you, depending on the purpose and hardware limitations.

  • To begin, the essential library required is the Transformers package developed by Hugging Face. While this library allows for model loading, it’s important to note that the loaded model will not be compressed.
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
import transformers
import torch
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf")
pipeline = transformers.pipeline(
"text-generation",
model="meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf",
torch_dtype=torch.float16,
device_map="auto",
)
  • You can also use sharding, a way to chunk into small pieces (depending on your limitations) the model you want to use. It can be done using the Accelerate library to keep the model in small pieces. However, to load the model, you would need to use the Fairscale library to load a model in shards for inference or training. Check the documentation for more information about the fully sharded data parallel method.
  • Then, you can use the BitsandBytes library, which will perform quantization on your model loading, changing the number of bits of memory used by the model. This powerful technique reduces the memory requirement to load a model without sacrificing its performance. You can check here for more technical details.
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig

model_id = "meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf"
bnb_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
    load_in_4bit=True,
    bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,
    bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16
)

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, quantization_config=bnb_config, device_map={"":0})
  • Finally, you can use post-quantization techniques such as GPTQ, auto-GPTQ, ANQ, or the GGUF method. Each one has its own pros and cons. The choice depends on the model you are using, your machine components (CPU, GPU, and GPU size), and the balance between compression and accuracy of the model that you want to keep.

GPTQ, tailored for GPT models, post-quantizes weights during fine-tuning. Choose between BitsAndBytes and GPTQ based on your specific needs: BitsAndBytes for general-purpose quantization in transformer models, and GPTQ for GPT-specific quantization. The auto-GPTQ library in Hugging Face’s transformers is suitable for large language models with encoder or decoder architectures like Llama, OPT, GPT-Neo, and GPT-NeoX. You can also find the implementation of auto-GPTQ for different models developed by The Bloke, who created more than 3000 implementations of different quantizations with other models. Additionally, ANQ (Action Weight Quantization) prioritizes significant weights based on activation and can be accessed through the vllm package. GGUP (GPT-Generated Unified Format) optimizes CPU usage by utilizing GPU only for specific layers to speed up the process, accessible via the transformers package.

Select your preferred model and load the suitable version, optimizing with the right quantization standard for compression/accuracy balance. Utilize a Hugging Face transformer pipeline: quantize, tokenize, and integrate into Langchain’s workflow efficiently.

pipeline = pipeline(
    task='text-generation',
    model=model,
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    return_full_text=True,  # needed by langchain
    # model params
    max_new_tokens=512,
    temperature=0.1,  # creativity of responses: 0.0 none ->  1.0 max
    repetition_penalty=1.1  # to avoid repeating output
)

2. Embeddings: Personalizing the Model

You want to personalize your agent. At this step, you have two possibilities again. You can add documents (webpage, raw text, pdf*…) and transform those documents into embeddings that you will evaluate using an existing embedding space (here, all-mpnet-base-v2). You can then store those new data in a vector store. To do so, you need to charge the proper embeddings for your task, load your documents, tokenize them, and calculate them before charging the results using Faiss or Chroma.

from langchain.document_loaders import PyPDFLoader 
from langchain.text_splitter import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter


pdf_path = "YourPDF.pdf"
documents =  PyPDFLoader(pdf_path).load_and_split()


#Cut your pdf file into smaller text chunks
text_splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
  chunk_size=1000,
  chunk_overlap=20
)

chunked_documents = text_splitter.split_documents(documents)
from langchain.embeddings import HuggingFaceEmbeddings
from langchain.vectorstores import FAISS

model_name = "sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2"
model_kwargs = {'device': 'cpu'}
encode_kwargs = {'normalize_embeddings': False}
embeddings = HuggingFaceEmbeddings(
    model_name=model_name,
    model_kwargs=model_kwargs,
    encode_kwargs=encode_kwargs
)
# storing embeddings in the vector store
vectorstore = FAISS.from_documents(texts, embeddings)

As it is the primary type that we will feed the model in the following article, here is a little glimpse of information concerning PDF reading and loading into an LLM. PDF reading poses challenges, with various packages available for tasks like decoding images into text. Errors in PDF interpretation can have significant consequences, particularly in sensitive contexts like financial summaries. Human intervention remains crucial for quality control, highlighting the need to oversee information generated by language models. For further insights, refer here and here.

3. Alternative Fine-Tuning with LoRA

Consider using Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) for large pre-trained models. Traditional fine-tuning methods are costly due to the vast number of parameters. Instead, opt for techniques like low-rank adaptation (LoRA), which adapts a smaller subset of parameters, reducing the computational burden and overfitting risks. LoRA projects hidden states into a lower-dimensional space for adaptation before projecting them back. It enhances efficiency and performance across tasks like text classification and language translation for models like GPT-3.

from peft import prepare_model_for_kbit_training
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model
from datasets import load_dataset

#Prepare the model for fine-tuning training with peft method
model.gradient_checkpointing_enable()
model = prepare_model_for_kbit_training(model)

def print_trainable_parameters(model):
    """
    Prints the number of trainable parameters in the model.
    """
    trainable_params = 0
    all_param = 0
    for _, param in model.named_parameters():
        all_param += param.numel()
        if param.requires_grad:
            trainable_params += param.numel()
    print(
        f"trainable params: {trainable_params} || all params: {all_param} || trainable%: {100 * trainable_params / all_param}"
    )


#Use LoRA
config = LoraConfig(
    r=8, 
    lora_alpha=32, 
    target_modules=["query_key_value"], 
    lora_dropout=0.05, 
    bias="none", 
    task_type="CAUSAL_LM"
)

model = get_peft_model(model, config)
print_trainable_parameters(model)

4. Conversational Retrieval Chain: Interactive Querying

A crucial aspect of any AI assistant is its ability to engage in meaningful conversations with users. Leveraging a conversational retrieval chain, we can enable our assistant to answer both model-based and embedding-based queries, providing comprehensive and relevant responses. This integration empowers users to interact with the assistant naturally and intuitively.

You can test your agent before deployment by using a Langchain conversational retriever chain that will use both the model and the embeddings to answer your question. Interestingly, the RAG retrieval generation model uses both retrieval-based and generative answers.

from langchain.chains import ConversationalRetrievalChain
from langchain import PromptTemplate
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate

custom_template = """You work for CompanyX which sells things located in United States.
        If you don't know the answer, just say that you don't. Don't try to make up an answer.
        Base your questions only on the knowledge provided here. Do not use any outside knowledge.
        Given the following chat history and a follow up question, 
        rephrase the follow up question to be a standalone question, 
        in its original language.
        Chat History:
        {chat_history}
        Follow Up Input: {question}
        Standalone question:
      """
      
custom_prompt_from_template = PromptTemplate.from_template(custom_template)

memory = ConversationBufferMemory(memory_key="chat_history", input_key="question", return_messages=True)
    
chain = ConversationalRetrievalChain.from_llm(
  llm,
  vectorstore.as_retriever(),
  condense_question_prompt=custom_prompt_from_template,
  memory=memory,
  response_if_no_docs_found="I don't know"
)

Analyze prompts closely; they adhere to structured standards, unlike natural conversations. Adhering to these standards is essential for effective response from the model. There are some resources to automatically optimize prompts, such as APO (Automatic Prompt Optimization) or AutoPrompt. You can also check this resource for the keys to better prompting or this article!

5. Wrapping the Agent: Interface Integration

To bring our personalized AI assistant to life, we must wrap it with an interface that facilitates user interaction after model deployment. Options with Langchain, Gradio, or Streamlit offer versatile solutions for integrating our assistant into various applications and platforms, ensuring seamless user engagement across different environments.

And voila! You should have a customized personal agent to feed with particular tasks! As always, all code shared here will soon be available in a GitHub repository for your exploration and experimentation.

Keep creating!

Extra resources on the topic :

An exciting personal agent API using Streamlit as your personal agent: https://github.com/phidatahq/phidata/tree/main/cookbook/llms/ollama/auto_rag

Developing Apps with GPT-4 and ChatGPT: https://learning.oreilly.com/library/view/developing-apps-with/9781098152475/ch05.html#memory_idKsxZI5

https://analyticsindiamag.com/meta-launches-open-source-models-openai-controls-them/

Langflow for Lanchain with visual coding using nodes: https://cobusgreyling.medium.com/langflow-for-langchain-58c143ba9218

Designing Large Language Model Applications, a new book from O’Reilly edition that is available in preview for some chapters: //learning.oreilly.com/library/view/designing-large-language/9781098150495/ch01.html#id77

An article about the open-source terminology problematic use for Llama and chat-Gpt: https://spectrum.ieee.org/open-source-llm-not-open

Another one pondering the pros and cons of open-source and close-source LLM: https://springsapps.com/knowledge/open-source-vs-closed-source-llms-pros-and-cons

entry.title: The Art of Tomorrow: AI-Infused Projection Mapping Proof Of Concept!

link.title: The Art of Tomorrow: AI-Infused Projection Mapping Proof Of Concept!

entry.content:
Growing up in a city neighboring Lyon, France, I’ve been fortunate to witness the celebrated “Fête des Lumières” firsthand. This captivating annual occasion bathes Lyon in an exquisite showcase of light, metamorphosing its thoroughfares, iconic sites, and edifices into awe-inspiring masterpieces. Each year, millions of visitors from around the globe flock to witness this extraordinary spectacle, immersing themselves in the enchanting realm of light, color, and innovation that defines the Fête des Lumières.

Today, I decided to embark on a personal challenge: using Houdini, a 3D software, to create and simulate a light art installation reminiscent of those seen at the “Fête des Lumières”. This idea has been brewing in my mind for quite some time; I’ve envisioned a unique approach. I aimed to place the visitor at the center of the experience by incorporating an onsite prompt system. This system would dynamically generate the projected image over the building based on prompts provided by visitors, utilizing generative AI technology. With that match plan in mind, let’s see how we can create a proof of concept that does this.

In a previous article, I demonstrated the use of SideFx Houdini software to generate AI-generated images through the MLOPs package. You can have a look into the detailed explanation in the previous article (here) to grasp the fundamentals of my Stable Diffusion image generation workflow. In this article, I’ll delve deeper into additional aspects of the process, building upon the groundwork laid out previously.

First things first, let’s found a 3D model worth of our inspiration. On my side, I’ve settled on using a 3D model of the door from the French medieval church of Sainte-Radegonde (Poitiers). The model is freely available for download (here).

Now that we’ve downloaded and imported our model into Houdini, we will apply a series of transformations to align it with the viewport grid. We then split the mesh into Houdini groups, which we’ll later use to populate a custom attribute named “building_parts”. This attribute will prove useful shortly when we delve into the generative AI step, as it will be used to create masks I will use to merge all our generated AI layers using compositing.

For this proof of concept, we’ve limited ourselves to three zones of interest: the main door group, encompassing all areas within the arch; the sidewalls, consisting of the two side columns and the main wall; essentially everything else. At that point, our setup that handles the mesh looks like the one below.

Now, we return to Houdini root at the “/obj” level and create a camera and a point light, which we’ll utilize as a gobo light to project our image. Additionally, we set up an environment light. Finally, as demonstrated in our previous article, we import our image-generative AI workflow. At that point, our “/obj” level looks like this.

We established the camera resolution at 512x512, which serves as the maximum resolution input image for the stable diffusion model.

As illustrated in the preceding screenshot, a critical procedure involved configuring the camera settings to attain consistent viewpoints between the camera and the gobo-equipped point light. This alignment is essential because we want the image projected from the gobo to match what has been captured by the camera.

Now, let’s explore the generative AI step further. Within our “/obj/sd” node, we’ll create three separate graphs, each tasked with generating an image for a specific part of the segmented mesh using the custom attribute “building_parts” we established earlier. This segmentation enables us to tailor the generative AI process to each distinct area of interest in the scene, ensuring precise and targeted image generation.

This means we use the same design to build three different prompt and model architectures for the doors or arch, the mainwall, and the sidewalls. Below is the design explained for the door area.

We connect all of those branches back using a merge node and connect this later one to a Python SOP node. This Python node will refresh the loading of the COP nodes, which will load the generated AI image residing within the “cop2net” node below. Once each branch has finished generating an image, this refresh triggers an update in the compositing process, consequently updating the projected image at the gobo level. This linkage is dynamic, as it’s directly associated with our “cop2net” node's final output node.

Above is the design for the cop2net node, showing the different stages of implementation of the stable diffusion images and the masks from the attributes into composite images. This leads to the final output image.

Next, we set the gobo light’s “Projection Map” parameter to dynamically retrieve the image directly from the cop2net1 node using the following expression “op:/obj/sd/cop2net1/OUT/”.

We also enable the viewport’s high-quality lighting option (the bulb button on the left) and select “Show All Objects” from the top viewport button options. This ensures we can accurately preview the scene’s lighting and overall appearance in real-time feedback.

Here is an example of a new door style when applying the code and the different steps of scene view options:

For another prompt (“luxurious and vibrant tropical forest plants with vivid colored flowers, very detailed and lots of red, orange, greens”, we created a gif resulting from multiple output from the stable diffusion.

Of course, it is a proof of concept and the quality could be enhanced with better lighting, different testing with the parameters, we could use a new version of the stable diffusion model. As always, there is a lot of space for improvement in machine learning projects and that is the beauty of it!

Consider the excitement of a light festival and envision the endless possibilities if participants could directly engage with various elements of the lighting spectacle. The interactivity would provide so much excitement. The potential for innovation knows no bounds; all it takes is a single prompt to unleash boundless creativity.

As always, all Houdini scenes shared here will soon be available in a GitHub repository for your exploration and experimentation. Keep creating!

entry.title: Unlocking the Hidden Potential of Houdini with MLOPs

link.title: Unlocking the Hidden Potential of Houdini with MLOPs

entry.content:
Recently, I encountered new challenges and decided to experiment with Houdini from SideFx. Houdini is a node-based 3D software widely utilized for creating visual effects in films and TV series. It facilitates robust procedural workflows and provides functionality for users to create, share, and sell their tools.

Today, I want to focus on one such tool called MLOPs (Machine Learning Operators), which has recently gained popularity within the Houdini community. I’ll walk you through my workflow for generating Stable Diffusion images and share some neat tricks you can employ to create a seamless progression of images with consistent themes or styles.

After following the installation instructions provided on the MLOPs GitHub page, I’ve configured the following base MLOPs scene within a Geometry node to produce an image from a text prompt, utilizing the default MLOPs Stable Diffusion 1.5 model.

In our setup, we’ve configured the seed to be determined by the current frame value ($F). This approach enables us to efficiently generate variations of the image our Stable Diffusion model produces simply by playing through the frame range.

A neat trick that could be employed after generating the initial image is to input the previously generated image into the second “sd text encoder” node and constrain the model hyperparameters to utilize it for generating the following image.

Animating the ‘Hue Shift’ and allowing the model to run for 70 frames resulted in this output.

This concludes our introduction to using MLOPs in Houdini to generate images. I hope this article will inspire you to embark on creative exploration within Houdini using this powerful tool. If you ever want to enrich your understanding further, there are plenty of amazing videos out there on YouTube from MLOPs creators Moritz Schwind (aka Entagma) and Paul Ambrosiussen.

Stay tuned, as I’ll write another MLOPs article to demonstrate how this workflow can be enhanced. This could pave the way for creating basic building projection mapping art installations that respond to onsite user prompts. If this piques your curiosity, the article is accessible here.

As always, all Houdini scenes shared here will be available soon on a git repository for your exploration and experimentation.

Keep creating!
